subject: Stratification - poor performance in one of three strata

messages.author: 60ed19f83201f725
messages.subject: Stratification - poor performance in one of three strata
parts:
Hello List -
I am analyzing a multi-species avian data set where transects of point
count stations were laid out in three habitats. I am analyzing each
species separately with the data set stratified by habitat (detection
function estimated by stratum). Most species do well in this situation
with models performing good or well for all three habitats/stratum.

The exception is AMROs (American Robins). This species gives me funky
results and I would appreciate some help on analysis strategy. So far I
have run through several models after variable truncation points which
reduced the data set by about 12% as suggested. Without bins AIC values
were in the 3000s. After using bins, the AIC values are in the 900s. A
seemly good improvement as there was evidence of heaping. The problem I am
having is that the models seem to work really well for two habitats and
relatively poorly for the third (bimodal detection probability with poor
chi square and a high CV - very high CV 42%) even though it has the best
AIC value. I was going to choose a model with a higher AIC value that
resulted in better fit of the detection probability for all three habitat
types. Is this the best route or do I fuss with the bins until I find the
best performer for all three habitats based on Chi-square, AIC, and CV? Or,
do I try a different approach such as using habitat as a covariate or
independently analyze each habitat? If I try a different approach, should
I use it for all species in the data set? Most importantly, can I truly
compare habitat density estimates for a single species across habitats that
used different models to estimate density within the habitats? I think I am
getting confused by the plethora of options. Thank you for the help! KB

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Stratification - poor performance in one of three strata
parts:
Kristin, AIC values can only be compared if you have the same data, so for
example you can't use AIC to decide whether you should group your data or
not. The easy guide to this is that you can compare AIC values in
Distance only if the different runs used the same data filter.

Sometimes by chance, data will exhibit a shape that doesn't reflect the
true detection function very well. In that case, you may well get an
implausible fit coming out with the best AIC. If the fitted detection
function simply isn't a plausible shape, given your understanding of the
detection process and your experience with other similar data sets, then
you should consider going with another model fit. Having the same model
fitted independently in each stratum makes sense, and you might then
choose to go with the model that gives the smallest summed AIC.

You might also consider using the MCDS engine of Distance, with either
habitat or stratum as a factor-type covariate. Then in the estimate tab
of the model definition tick for detection function both stratum and
global. This tells Distance to fit a single model across strata, but
allow a different scale parameter for each stratum.

Steve Buckland
